1.name: Documented historical influence
1.desc: Direct influence documented in the historical record.

2.name: Textual transmission or adaptation
2.desc: A text was translated, edited, published or adapted by the later party.

3.name: Philosophical relationship
3.desc: A shared or developed philosophical idea, without a claim of direct influence.

4.name: Educational prerequisite
4.desc: Understanding the first is needed to study the second in this curriculum.

5.name: Practical application
5.desc: The second applies the first in practice.

6.name: Comparative symbolic relationship
6.desc: A parallel drawn by comparison; not a claim of historical transmission.

1.title: The intellectual relationship map
1.caption: An overview of the historical and philosophical network: traditions, authors, texts and concepts placed by approximate date and by current. Line styles show the kind of relationship. The interactive map lets you select any node and follow its influences.
1.desc: A wide chart with nine horizontal bands labelled Philosophy and theurgy, Hermetic and Renaissance philosophy, Astrology natural and folk magic, Kabbalah and Qabalah, Alchemy and Rosicrucianism, Freemasonry, Ceremonial magic, Comparative esotericism and Tarot. Time runs from antiquity on the left to the present on the right. Dots for traditions, authors, texts and concepts are joined by lines of six styles for six kinds of relationship. Ceremonial magic, the Golden Dawn and Hermetic Tarot receive lines from many earlier currents.

2.title: The nine-stage educational progression
2.caption: The Solitary Study ascends from the Gate of Light through eight further stages and then returns to its beginning. The recommended durations total about forty-two months; they are recommendations, not requirements.
2.desc: Nine numbered circles rise from lower left to upper right: I Porta Lucis, The Gate of Light, 3 months; II Philosophia, The Nature of Reality, 6 months; III Scientia Hermetica, The Science of Correspondence, 4 months; IV Natura Arcana, The Hidden Virtues of Nature, 4 months; V Arbor Vitae, The Tree of Life, 6 months; VI Rosa Crucis, The Mystery of Regeneration, 4 months; VII Ars Magica, The Sacred Art, 8 months; VIII Lingua Mysteriorum, The Language of the Mysteries, 4 months; IX Verbum Perditum, The Lost Word, 3 months. A curved arrow returns from IX to I, labelled the return.

3.title: The Council relationship network
3.caption: The selected authors of the Council arranged around a circle by current, with direct documented relationships between authors drawn as lines. Inclusion is an editorial selection by Greco Arcana and implies no affiliation or endorsement.
3.desc: A circle of author names grouped by current: philosophy, Hermetic and Renaissance philosophy, natural magic and astrology, Qabalah, Rosicrucian and alchemical writers, Masonic writers, ceremonial magicians, comparative esotericists and Tarot authors. Inner Council authors have filled markers, Outer Council authors open markers. Lines connect authors with documented relationships, such as Plotinus to Iamblichus, Ficino to Agrippa, Agrippa to Dee, Lévi to Pike, Crowley to Regardie and Regardie to the Ciceros.

4.title: Masonic initiation and symbolic interpretation
4.caption: Four levels at which a symbol of the Craft can be read, illustrated with the rough ashlar. The literal and moral readings are given in Masonic lectures; the philosophical and esoteric readings are the subject of this curriculum.
4.desc: Four concentric rings around a drawing of a rough stone. From the outer ring inward: Literal, a stone as it comes from the quarry; Moral, the imperfect nature of the candidate to be improved by education and discipline; Philosophical, matter not yet shaped by form, in Platonic terms; Esoteric, the soul's rectification, compared with the alchemist's prima materia. Labels on the right repeat the four readings.
4.refs: Mackey, The Symbolism of Freemasonry; Wilmshurst, The Meaning of Masonry

5.title: Plato, Plotinus and Neoplatonic metaphysics
5.caption: The Platonic frame (left) and its Neoplatonic systematization (right). Reality proceeds downward from the One; the soul returns upward. The parallel is a simplification for study.
5.desc: Two vertical columns. Left, Plato: the Good; the Forms; the World Soul; the visible cosmos. Right, Plotinus: the One; Intellect (Nous), containing the Forms; Soul, including the World Soul and individual souls; Nature and the material world; Matter. A downward arrow on the far right is labelled procession; an upward arrow on the far left is labelled return.
5.refs: Plato, Republic VI–VII and Timaeus; Plotinus, Enneads V.1 and VI.9

6.title: Procession, participation and return
6.caption: Proclus's triad: every effect remains in its cause, proceeds from it and returns to it. Participation is the relationship that makes the effect like its cause.
6.desc: A circle with three stations. At the top, Remaining (monē): the effect pre-exists in its cause. On the right, Procession (proodos): the effect goes forth and becomes distinct. On the left, Return (epistrophē): the effect turns back toward its source. Arrows run clockwise around the circle. In the center: Participation, the effect shares in what its cause is.

7.title: The five Platonic solids
7.caption: The five regular solids and the elements assigned to them in Plato's Timaeus. Plato reserved the fifth, the dodecahedron, for the whole cosmos. Drawn in simplified projection.
7.desc: Five geometric solids drawn in line. Tetrahedron: 4 triangular faces, Fire. Octahedron: 8 triangular faces, Air. Icosahedron: 20 triangular faces, Water. Cube: 6 square faces, Earth. Dodecahedron: 12 pentagonal faces, used by the god for the whole cosmos.

8.title: Macrocosm and microcosm
8.caption: The structural parallel at the heart of Hermetic philosophy: the threefold universe and the threefold human being. The pairing follows the common Renaissance scheme; individual authors differ in detail.
8.desc: Two concentric diagrams side by side joined by dashed lines. Left, the macrocosm: the divine or intellectual world at the center of honor, the celestial world of the stars and seven planets, and the elemental world of fire, air, water and earth. Right, the microcosm: mind, the spirit or soul, and the body. Dashed lines connect divine world with mind, celestial world with soul and spirit, elemental world with body.
8.refs: Corpus Hermeticum; Agrippa, De occulta philosophia; Fludd, Utriusque Cosmi Historia (1617)

9.title: Agrippa's three worlds
9.caption: Agrippa arranges occult philosophy in three books for three worlds. Virtues descend from the higher worlds into the lower; the magician seeks to ascend through them.
9.desc: Three stacked bands. Top: the intellectual world, Book III, ceremonial magic: angels and intelligences, divine names, religion. Middle: the celestial world, Book II, celestial and mathematical magic: stars and planets, number, harmony and proportion. Bottom: the elemental world, Book I, natural magic: elements, stones, metals, plants and animals. A downward arrow on the right reads virtues descend; an upward arrow on the left reads the magician ascends.
9.refs: Agrippa, De occulta philosophia libri tres (1533), I–III

10.title: Elemental correspondences
10.caption: The four elements arranged by their two qualities in the Aristotelian scheme, with the traditional humours, seasons, Platonic solids and the Tarot suits of the Golden Dawn tradition.
10.desc: A square with an element at each corner. Fire, hot and dry: choleric humour, summer, tetrahedron, Wands. Air, hot and wet: sanguine, spring, octahedron, Swords. Water, cold and wet: phlegmatic, winter, icosahedron, Cups. Earth, cold and dry: melancholic, autumn, cube, Pentacles. The sides of the square are labelled with the shared quality: hot, wet, cold, dry.
10.refs: Aristotle, On Generation and Corruption II; Plato, Timaeus; Golden Dawn Tarot attributions

11.title: The seven classical planets and their traditional correspondences
11.caption: The planets in their Chaldean order around the circle. Following the heptagram from the Sun yields the order of the days of the week. The table gives each planet's day, metal and Sephirah in the Hermetic Qabalah.
11.desc: A seven-pointed star inside a circle with the planets in Chaldean order clockwise from the top: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon. Arrows along the star lead Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, the order of the weekdays. A table lists: Saturn, Saturday, lead, Binah; Jupiter, Thursday, tin, Chesed; Mars, Tuesday, iron, Geburah; Sun, Sunday, gold, Tiphareth; Venus, Friday, copper, Netzach; Mercury, Wednesday, quicksilver, Hod; Moon, Monday, silver, Yesod.
11.refs: Agrippa, De occulta philosophia II; Golden Dawn attributions

12.title: Astrology and talismanic magic: a dependency map
12.caption: A traditional talisman is the meeting point of several kinds of knowledge, each studied at a different stage. The map shows what a single operation depends on.
12.desc: A flow chart. At the top, Cosmology: correspondence and the three worlds, Stages II and III. It feeds three boxes: Astrology, choosing the planet, election and hour, Stage IV; Natural magic, choosing the metal, stone and herb, Stage IV; Symbolism, choosing the image, character and divine name, Stages V and VII. Together with Intention and consecration, Stage VII, these converge on the talisman at the bottom.
12.refs: Ficino, De vita III; Agrippa, De occulta philosophia I–II; Warnock, Secrets of Planetary Magic

13.title: The historical development of Hermetic Qabalah
13.caption: Three distinct traditions on one timeline. Jewish Kabbalah, Renaissance Christian Cabala and the Hermetic Qabalah of the occult revival share a diagram but not a single meaning. Arrows mark documented transmission.
13.desc: A timeline in three lanes. Jewish Kabbalah: Sefer Yetzirah, 3rd to 6th century; Sefer ha-Bahir, about 1180; the Zohar, late 13th century; Moses Cordovero, Pardes Rimonim, 1548; Isaac Luria, Safed, 16th century. Christian Cabala: Pico della Mirandola, 900 Theses, 1486; Johannes Reuchlin, De arte cabalistica, 1517; Agrippa, 1533; Kircher, Oedipus Aegyptiacus, 1652 to 1654; Knorr von Rosenroth, Kabbala Denudata, 1677 to 1684. Hermetic Qabalah: Lévi, Dogme et rituel, 1854 to 1856; Westcott, Sepher Yetzirah, 1887; Mathers, The Kabbalah Unveiled, 1887; the Golden Dawn, 1888; Crowley, 777, 1909; Fortune, The Mystical Qabalah, 1935. Arrows lead from the Zohar to Pico, from Kabbala Denudata to Mathers, from Agrippa and Lévi to the Golden Dawn.
13.refs: Scholem, Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism (for the Jewish chronology); primary dates as given

14.title: The Tree of Life (interactive)
14.caption: The ten Sephiroth and twenty-two paths with the attributions used in the Hermetic Qabalah of the Golden Dawn tradition. Select a Sephirah or a path to see its correspondences. Angelic and divine-name attributions vary between sources; those shown follow the Golden Dawn.
14.desc: The Tree of Life: ten circles in three columns joined by twenty-two lines. Top to bottom: Kether, Crown; Chokmah, Wisdom, and Binah, Understanding; Chesed, Mercy, and Geburah, Severity; Tiphareth, Beauty; Netzach, Victory, and Hod, Splendour; Yesod, Foundation; Malkuth, Kingdom. Each path carries a Hebrew letter. The paths are numbered 11 to 32, from Aleph between Kether and Chokmah to Tav between Yesod and Malkuth.
14.refs: Sefer Yetzirah; Mathers, The Kabbalah Unveiled; Regardie, The Golden Dawn; Fortune, The Mystical Qabalah

15.title: The four Qabalistic worlds
15.caption: The four worlds of the Qabalah with the letters of the divine name, the elements and the Tarot suits attributed to them in the Hermetic Qabalah, and the beings associated with each world.
15.desc: Four horizontal tiers. Atziluth, the world of emanation: Yod, Fire, Wands, the divine names. Briah, the world of creation: Heh, Water, Cups, the archangels. Yetzirah, the world of formation: Vav, Air, Swords, the angelic choirs. Assiah, the world of action: final Heh, Earth, Pentacles, the planets and the material world.
15.refs: Hermetic Qabalah of the Golden Dawn tradition; Fortune, The Mystical Qabalah

16.title: Alchemy and Rosicrucian regeneration
16.caption: The four classical stages of the alchemical work around an original rose-cross emblem, with three ways of reading each stage. Laboratory, spiritual and psychological readings belong to different periods and should not be confused.
16.desc: A circle of four stations around a rose cross drawn as an original emblem. Nigredo, the blackening: in the laboratory, decomposition; spiritually, mortification; in psychological reading, confronting the shadow. Albedo, the whitening: purification; washing of the soul; reflection and clarity. Citrinitas, the yellowing: maturation; illumination; dawning insight. Rubedo, the reddening: completion of the Stone; regeneration; integration. A note says the rough ashlar becoming the perfect ashlar is a comparative parallel.
16.refs: Fama Fraternitatis (1614); Chymical Wedding (1616); Maier, Atalanta Fugiens (1617)

17.title: Origins and convergence of Golden Dawn ceremonial magic
17.caption: The currents that converged in the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn in 1888, and the principal lines that descend from it. Bardon and Miller are shown apart as independent operative approaches.
17.desc: Eight source boxes on the left: Neoplatonic theurgy; Hermeticism; Renaissance occult philosophy (Ficino, Agrippa); Christian Cabala and Hermetic Qabalah (Lévi); Enochian magic (Dee); astrology and natural magic; Rosicrucianism; Freemasonry and the Societas Rosicruciana in Anglia. Arrows converge on a central box: the Golden Dawn, 1888, Westcott, Mathers, Woodman. From it arrows lead to Crowley and Thelema; Waite; Fortune and the Inner Light; Case and the Builders of the Adytum; Regardie's publication 1937 to 1940, which leads to the Ciceros and other modern practitioners including Greer. Separate dashed boxes: Bardon, independent Hermetic training; Miller, contemporary practical magic.
17.refs: Regardie, The Golden Dawn; Gilbert, The Golden Dawn Companion; histories of the Order

18.title: The philosophical anatomy of the Lesser Ritual of the Pentagram
18.caption: The publicly published Lesser Ritual of the Pentagram analyzed into its components, each traced to the stage of the curriculum that explains it. Quarter attributions follow the Golden Dawn as published by Regardie.
18.desc: A large pentagram in a circle with the four quarters marked. East: the divine name YHVH, archangel Raphael, element Air. South: Adonai, Michael, Fire. West: Eheieh, Gabriel, Water. North: AGLA, Auriel, Earth. Above, the Qabalistic Cross: Ateh, thou art, at the forehead, Kether; Malkuth, the kingdom, at the feet; ve-Geburah, and the power, at the right shoulder; ve-Gedulah, and the glory, at the left shoulder; le-Olahm, Amen, forever. Side labels trace each part to its source: Qabalah and divine names, Stage V; elements, Stage IV; angelic tradition, Stage VII; geometry, Stage II; the pentagram as microcosm, Stage III; ritual as theurgy, Stage II.
18.refs: Regardie, The Golden Dawn (Neophyte grade material)

19.title: The historical development of Hermetic Tarot
19.caption: From a fifteenth-century Italian card game to the symbolic language of the Western mysteries. The occult reading of the cards is a documented development, not their origin.
19.desc: A timeline. About 1440, Italian trionfi cards, the earliest Tarot decks, made for games. 17th to 18th century, the Tarot de Marseille pattern. 1781, Court de Gébelin claims an Egyptian origin. 1780s, Etteilla publishes on cartomancy and a divinatory Tarot. 1854 to 1856, Lévi joins the trumps to the Hebrew letters. 1888 onward, the Golden Dawn revises the attributions and assigns the cards to the Tree, planets and decans. 1909, the Rider–Waite–Smith deck. 1944, Crowley and Harris, the Thoth Tarot. 1947, Case, The Tarot. 1980 onward, Pollack and Greer develop modern interpretation. A dividing line marks the move from game to occult interpretation in 1781.
19.refs: Huson, Mystical Origins of the Tarot; Waite, The Pictorial Key; Decker, Depaulis and Dummett, A Wicked Pack of Cards (for the history)

20.title: Tarot, Qabalah and astrology: the relationships
20.caption: How Hermetic Tarot maps the deck onto the Tree of Life and the heavens. The threefold division of the Hebrew letters comes from the Sefer Yetzirah; the attribution of cards to letters follows the Golden Dawn.
20.desc: Two panels. Left, the Major Arcana: 22 trumps equal 22 Hebrew letters equal 22 paths on the Tree; the letters divide into 3 mothers, attributed to the elements Air, Water and Fire; 7 doubles, attributed to the planets; 12 simples, attributed to the zodiac signs. Right, the Minor Arcana: four suits correspond to the four elements and four worlds; Aces to Tens correspond to the ten Sephiroth; the 36 small cards from Two to Ten correspond to the 36 decans of the zodiac; the 16 court cards are elemental subdivisions.
20.refs: Sefer Yetzirah; Golden Dawn, Book T; Case, The Tarot

21.title: The Three of Swords: a correspondence analysis
21.caption: Five layers of the Three of Swords in Hermetic Tarot, drawn from five different stages of the curriculum. Together they guide an interpretation rather than dictating a keyword.
21.desc: A central card outline labelled Three of Swords with five surrounding boxes. Number three: Binah, Understanding, the sphere of Saturn on the Tree of Life, Stage V. Suit: Swords, the element Air, the world of Yetzirah, Stage IV. Decan: Saturn in Libra, the second decan of Libra in the Golden Dawn system, Stage IV. Title: Lord of Sorrow, the Golden Dawn title of the card, Stage VII. Image: a heart pierced by three swords under storm clouds and rain, Rider–Waite–Smith 1909, Stage VIII. A line beneath summarizes: understanding that comes through sorrow; the mind's clarity tested by grief.
21.refs: Golden Dawn, Book T; Waite, The Pictorial Key; Case, The Tarot

22.title: The Great Work and the Masonic temple
22.caption: A comparative diagram: the threefold plan of Solomon's Temple set beside the stages of the Great Work and the ascent of the soul. The pairing is a Greco Arcana interpretation for study, not a doctrine of any Masonic body.
22.desc: A temple plan seen from above, entered from the east-facing porch at the bottom. The porch with two pillars, Jachin and Boaz; the holy place; the holy of holies. Beside each, three columns: the alchemical stage, the condition of the soul and the curriculum stages. Porch: nigredo, preparation, Stages I and II. Holy place: albedo and citrinitas, purification and illumination, Stages III to VI. Holy of holies: rubedo, union and regeneration, Stages VII to IX. Marked as a comparative interpretation.
22.refs: 1 Kings 6–7 (the Temple); comparative interpretation by Greco Arcana

23.title: Return to the Lost Word
23.caption: The integration of the curriculum: each stage supplies an instrument for investigating the allegory of the Craft, and the circle returns to its beginning.
23.desc: A circle of nine stations with the Lost Word at the center. I, the Gate of Light: allegory. II, the Nature of Reality: order. III, the Science of Correspondence: the microcosm. IV, the Hidden Virtues of Nature: the virtue of things. V, the Tree of Life: the divine names. VI, the Mystery of Regeneration: transformation. VII, the Sacred Art: operation. VIII, the Language of the Mysteries: the reading of images. IX, the Lost Word: integration, returning to I. Around the center: Freemasonry provides the allegory; the tradition provides the instruments; the Great Work is what the student does with them.
